llm_apis.notes: Vendor-neutral: requests, responses, tool calls and agents are shown as plain dicts/JSON in the OpenAI chat-completions shape (which OpenRouter and many local servers share); no network calls, every response is a canned JSON string or dict parsed locally. Sending the request over HTTP is not taught here: B16 apis_http/lib_requests (sibling) owns the HTTP client side; a stitch could add apis_http as an optional prerequisite of chat_request_messages KP4 or of lib_openai.client_and_chat_completion. API keys come from B13 environment_variables.secrets_out_of_code. context_window_budget has empty taught_in (added: tokens/cost/history trimming are what Boot.dev's verbose token printing hints at). Streaming, embeddings/RAG and image inputs were left out (no course teaches them).

lib_openai.notes: Two non-core topics. SDK snippets were NOT run (openai is not installed and no network calls were allowed); they are described, and everything after the SDK boundary works on response.model_dump() dicts so it is tested with fakes. Boot.dev's current AI Agent uses the OpenAI SDK against OpenRouter (base_url), earlier versions Google Gemini. pip install is a memorised line; third_party_packages.find_and_install is the prerequisite.

function_calling.notes: Owns tool schemas, reading tool_calls (arguments as a JSON string), dispatch via a dict of functions with ** (closes the reconcile GAP 'functions stored in a dict / dispatch table' for this domain) and the role 'tool' result messages. Anthropic-style tool_use/tool_result blocks differ only in key names; not shown separately.

ai_agents.notes: Boot.dev's toy coding agent: agent_loop (scripted fake models), sandboxed_file_tools (get_files_info/get_file_content/write_file guard), run_code_tool (run_python_file via subprocess; takes the B13 subprocess_module handoff), observe_and_test_agent (verbose flag, token totals, tests). human_approval_and_safety (approval prompts, prompt injection, limits) is not taught by any course (empty taught_in) but is essential for real agents. Multi-agent systems, memory stores and agent frameworks were left out.

markdown.notes: Follows Boot.dev's SSG: TextNode/TextType (dataclass + enum, so it needs B11 classes.dataclasses), split_nodes_delimiter, regex extraction (takes the B13 regular_expressions handoff, adds the (?<!!) lookbehind as one KP), split_nodes_image/link, text_to_textnodes, markdown_to_blocks and block_to_block_type. markdown_syntax introduces only the HTML tags needed; general HTML belongs to the web batches (B16/B17). Nested inline styles and the CommonMark spec are out of scope. Reconciliation review: the markdown (7) and static_site_generation (8) topics follow Boot.dev's static site generator project chapter by chapter. Kept as topics, but they form one guided project and are best delivered as multisteps (a project track) rather than as 15 independent lessons.

static_site_generation.notes: HTMLNode/LeafNode/ParentNode (inheritance + recursion, as B08 recursion's note asked), text_node_to_html (match on enums), markdown_to_html_node, recursive static copy (shutil memorised), page generation with str.replace templates (Jinja is B17 lib_jinja) and the build/preview/basepath script. Boot.dev renders as ; kept for consistency with LeafNode. Unit tests use plain assert (unit_testing.unittest_module is optional, non-core). Project-shaped: the whole build is a good multistep built on these topics. Reconciliation review: the markdown (7) and static_site_generation (8) topics follow Boot.dev's static site generator project chapter by chapter. Kept as topics, but they form one guided project and are best delivered as multisteps (a project track) rather than as 15 independent lessons.

topics.title: Chat requests: a model and a list of messages
topics.summary: Build the data for a chat-model request: a model name plus a list of role/content messages, including the conversation history the model needs.

knowledge_points.title: A request is a dict: model and messages
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values read out of a request dict; write the request for a given question and model name.

knowledge_points.title: Roles: system, user and assistant
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a terse assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2 + 2?"},
]
for m in messages:
    print(m["role"])  # system, then user
system sets the rules, user is the person, assistant is what the model said earlier.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the role for each piece of text (instructions, question, earlier reply); fix a message that uses the key 'text' instead of 'content'.

knowledge_points.title: The model remembers nothing: send the history
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2 + 2?"}]
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "4"})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "Double it."})
print(len(messages))  # 3
Each request must carry the whole conversation; 'Double it.' alone would mean nothing to the model.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the message list after several turns; fix a chat loop that sends only the newest user message.

knowledge_points.title: The request travels as JSON text
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the JSON text for a small request; spot why a request containing a Python set cannot be sent.

topics.title: Reading a chat response: reply text, finish reason and usage
topics.summary: Parse a chat-completion response (here a canned JSON string) and pull out the reply text, why the model stopped, the token usage, or the error message.

knowledge_points.title: Dig out the reply text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
raw = """{"choices": [{"message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "Bonjour!"},
  "finish_reason": "stop"}],
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 12, "completion_tokens": 3, "total_tokens": 15}}"""
data = json.loads(raw)
print(data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])  # Bonjour!
The reply sits in choices[0].message.content; that message can be appended to the history as it is.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the access path to the reply; predict the path's value for a response with two choices; append the reply to a messages list.

knowledge_points.title: finish_reason: complete or cut off
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the message for responses with different finish reasons; complete a check that warns on truncation.

knowledge_points.title: usage: how many tokens went in and out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
usage = data["usage"]
print(usage["prompt_tokens"], usage["completion_tokens"])  # 12 3
Tokens are word pieces; providers limit and bill by them, counting both the prompt and the reply.
knowledge_points.practice: Read token counts from responses; compute total tokens over three canned responses.

knowledge_points.title: Errors come back in a different shape
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
data = json.loads('{"error": {"message": "Invalid API key", "code": 401}}')
if "error" in data:
    print("API error:", data["error"]["message"])
else:
    print(data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# API error: Invalid API key
Check for an error before digging; data['choices'] here would raise KeyError.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output for success and error responses; fix code that crashes with KeyError on an error response.

topics.title: Shaping replies: system prompts, examples and settings
topics.summary: Steer a model with a system prompt, few-shot example turns, temperature and max_tokens, and wrap request building in a function.

knowledge_points.title: temperature and max_tokens
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Is 'great film' pos or neg?"}]
request = {"model": "some-model", "messages": messages,
           "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 5}
print(request["temperature"], request["max_tokens"])  # 0 5
temperature 0 gives the most repeatable answer, higher values more varied ones; max_tokens caps the reply length.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose settings for a classifier, a story writer and a one-word answer; predict which reply would end with finish_reason 'length'.

knowledge_points.title: A function that builds requests
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the request a call produces; add a max_tokens parameter with a default.

knowledge_points.title: Few-shot: show examples as earlier turns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Label the review pos or neg. One word."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Loved it"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "pos"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Waste of money"},
]
print(messages[-1]["role"])  # user
The made-up user/assistant pair shows the exact format wanted; the model continues the pattern.
knowledge_points.practice: Order shuffled messages into a valid few-shot prompt; add a second example pair to a list.

knowledge_points.title: Precise prompts: say the format and the limits
knowledge_points.worked_example:
vague = "Tell me about this review."
precise = ("Classify the review as pos or neg. "
           "Reply with exactly one word, lowercase, no punctuation.")
print(len(precise) > len(vague))  # True
A reply your code will parse needs its format spelled out; vague prompts get chatty answers.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the prompt most likely to give parseable output; rewrite a vague prompt to name the format and length.

topics.title: Asking for JSON and parsing the reply safely
topics.summary: Ask a model for JSON, then parse and check the reply, coping with code fences, invalid JSON and missing or wrong fields.

knowledge_points.title: Parse a JSON reply with json.loads
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
reply = '{"sentiment": "neg", "score": 0.9}'
result = json.loads(reply)
print(result["sentiment"], result["score"])  # neg 0.9
Ask in the prompt for JSON with named keys; the reply content is just a string until you parse it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict fields read from parsed replies; write the prompt line that names the keys you need.

knowledge_points.title: Remove code fences around the JSON
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
reply = '```json\n{"sentiment": "pos"}\n```'
text = reply.strip().removeprefix("```json").removesuffix("```")
print(json.loads(text)["sentiment"])  # pos
Models often wrap JSON in ```json fences; removeprefix/removesuffix cut text only if it is there.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the cleaned string; fix code that calls json.loads on a fenced reply.

knowledge_points.title: Invalid JSON: catch JSONDecodeError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict parse_reply results for good and bad replies; complete the except line.

knowledge_points.title: Check the fields before trusting them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = parse_reply('{"sentiment": "meh"}')
if data is None or data.get("sentiment") not in ("pos", "neg"):
    print("Bad reply, ask again")  # Bad reply, ask again
Valid JSON can still have missing keys or unexpected values; validate before use.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which replies pass the check; write a validator requiring a numeric 'score' between 0 and 1.

topics.title: Tokens, cost and the context window
topics.summary: Estimate tokens and cost from usage numbers, see why resending history grows every request, and trim old turns to stay inside the context window.

knowledge_points.title: Estimate tokens from characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog."
print(len(text) // 4)  # 11
English averages about 4 characters per token; exact counts need the model's own tokenizer (the usage field reports them).
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate tokens for strings of given lengths; choose whether a 600 000-character book fits a 128 000-token window.

knowledge_points.title: Cost from usage and prices
knowledge_points.worked_example:
usage = {"prompt_tokens": 1200, "completion_tokens": 300}
price_in = 0.50    # dollars per million input tokens (example price)
price_out = 1.50   # dollars per million output tokens
cost = (usage["prompt_tokens"] * price_in + usage["completion_tokens"] * price_out) / 1000000
print(cost)  # 0.00105
Input and output tokens usually have different prices; check the provider's price list.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute costs for given usage and prices; fix a formula that forgets to divide by a million.

knowledge_points.title: History makes every request bigger
knowledge_points.worked_example:
prompt_sizes = [50, 120, 210, 330]   # prompt_tokens of 4 turns
total = 0
for size in prompt_sizes:
    total += size
print(total)  # 710
Each turn resends everything before it, so total input tokens grow much faster than the conversation.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill a trace table of prompt tokens per turn when each turn adds 60 tokens; compute the running total.

knowledge_points.title: Trim old turns, keep the system prompt
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def trim(messages, keep=2):
    return messages[:1] + messages[-keep:]

msgs = ["system", "u1", "a1", "u2", "a2", "u3"]
print(trim(msgs))  # ['system', 'a2', 'u3']
The system prompt stays first; only the newest turns are kept. (Strings stand in for message dicts.)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict trim results for different keep values; fix a version that drops the system prompt.

topics.title: Calling a model with the OpenAI Python SDK
topics.summary: Install the openai package, create a client with the key from an environment variable, call chat.completions.create and read the reply with attributes; point the same code at another OpenAI-compatible provider.

knowledge_points.title: Install, import, create a client
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# $ python3 -m pip install openai
import os
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"])
(Not run here: needs the openai package, a key and the network.) The key comes from the environment, never from the source code.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the setup lines; spot the line that leaks a key.

knowledge_points.title: chat.completions.create sends the request
knowledge_points.worked_example:
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi in French"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)  # e.g. Bonjour !
(Not run here: needs the openai package, a key and the network.) The keyword arguments are exactly the request dict from llm_apis; the SDK does the HTTP.
knowledge_points.practice: Turn a request dict into a create(...) call; fill in the missing keyword argument.

knowledge_points.title: Read the response with dots, not brackets
knowledge_points.worked_example:
response.choices[0].message.content    # like data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
response.choices[0].finish_reason      # "stop" or "length"
response.usage.prompt_tokens           # like data["usage"]["prompt_tokens"]
response.model_dump()                  # the same data as a plain dict
(Not run here: needs the openai package, a key and the network.) The SDK returns objects whose attributes mirror the JSON keys; model_dump() turns one back into a dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate dict paths into attribute paths and back; fix response['choices'] (TypeError: not subscriptable).

knowledge_points.title: Same code, another provider: base_url
knowledge_points.worked_example:
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"],
)
(Not run here: needs the openai package, a key and the network.) Many providers (OpenRouter, local servers) speak the same API; only the URL, key and model names change.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose what must change to switch providers; write the client line for a local server URL.

topics.title: Wrapping the SDK: errors, retries and testing without the network
topics.summary: Hide the SDK behind one function, pass that function in so a fake can replace it in tests, handle the SDK's error types and test a retry loop with a fake that fails.

knowledge_points.title: One function talks to the SDK
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which parts of a program should import openai; complete the wrapper's return line.

knowledge_points.title: Pass the model function in; test with a fake
knowledge_points.practice: Predict ask() with different fakes; write a fake that returns a given canned reply and an assert that tests ask().

knowledge_points.title: Catch the SDK's errors, specific ones first
knowledge_points.practice: Order except clauses correctly; choose which errors are worth retrying (rate limit yes, bad key no).

knowledge_points.title: Test a retry loop with a fake that fails once
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output with fakes that fail 0, 2 and 3 times; write asserts for the give-up case.

topics.title: Describing your functions to a model: tool schemas
topics.summary: Write a tool definition (name, description, JSON Schema parameters) for a Python function and add tools to a chat request.

knowledge_points.title: A tool: name, description, parameters
knowledge_points.practice: Read fields out of a tool definition; fill in the name and description for a given def line.

knowledge_points.title: JSON Schema types for parameters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# def get_files_info(directory: str, max_items: int, hidden: bool)

properties = {
    "directory": {"type": "string", "description": "Folder, relative to the project"},
    "max_items": {"type": "integer"},
    "hidden": {"type": "boolean"},
}
str -> string, int -> integer, float -> number, bool -> boolean, list -> array; the hints tell you which.
knowledge_points.practice: Match Python hints to schema types; write the properties for a three-parameter function.

knowledge_points.title: Required and optional parameters, and tools in the request
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather_tool as defined in KP1
request = {"model": "some-model", "tools": [weather_tool],
           "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is it warm in Oslo?"}]}
print(len(request["tools"]))  # 1
Parameters with defaults are left out of required; the tools list goes next to messages.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the required list for functions with defaults; add a second tool to a request.

knowledge_points.title: Check a schema for mistakes
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug in schemas with mismatched names or Python type names; predict check_tool's output.

topics.title: Reading the tool calls in a response
topics.summary: Recognise a reply that asks for tool calls, read each call's id, function name and JSON-string arguments, and tell it apart from a final text answer.

knowledge_points.title: A reply that asks for a tool
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
data = {"choices": [{"finish_reason": "tool_calls", "message": {
    "role": "assistant", "content": None,
    "tool_calls": [{"id": "call_1", "type": "function",
        "function": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": '{"city": "Paris"}'}}]}}]}
message = data["choices"][0]["message"]
print(data["choices"][0]["finish_reason"], message["content"])  # tool_calls None
print(message["tool_calls"][0]["function"]["name"])  # get_weather
Instead of text, the model returns tool_calls: requests for your program to run functions. (data is a canned response after json.loads.)
knowledge_points.practice: Read names and ids from canned tool-call responses; predict finish_reason and content.

knowledge_points.title: arguments is a JSON string: parse it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
call = message["tool_calls"][0]
args = call["function"]["arguments"]
print(args["city"])  # TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'
args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
print(args["city"])  # Paris
The arguments arrive as JSON text, not a dict; json.loads them first.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that indexes the arguments string; predict the dict that json.loads returns for given arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Several calls in one reply
knowledge_points.worked_example:
calls = [
    {"id": "call_1", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": '{"city": "Paris"}'}},
    {"id": "call_2", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": '{"city": "Oslo"}'}},
]
for call in calls:
    print(call["id"], json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])["city"])
# call_1 Paris
# call_2 Oslo
A reply may request several calls at once; handle every one, keeping each id.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the loop's output for 1-3 calls; write a loop collecting the function names.

knowledge_points.title: Tool call or final answer?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def tool_calls_in(message):
    return message.get("tool_calls") or []

print(tool_calls_in({"role": "assistant", "content": "It is 18C."}))  # []
print(len(tool_calls_in(message)))  # 1
A final answer has no tool_calls key (or None); 'or []' turns both into an empty list you can loop over.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify canned replies as tool request or final answer; fix code that loops over message['tool_calls'] on a text reply.

topics.title: Running the function the model asked for
topics.summary: Map tool names to Python functions with a dict, call them with the parsed arguments, and turn unknown names and bad arguments into error text instead of crashes.

knowledge_points.title: The tool registry is a dispatch table
knowledge_points.practice: Predict calls through a dispatch dict; add a second tool to it.

knowledge_points.title: Call with ** and the parsed arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
args = json.loads('{"city": "Oslo"}')
print(TOOLS["get_weather"](**args))  # 18C in Oslo
**args passes each key as a keyword argument, so the schema's property names must match the parameter names.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of ** calls; fix a call that passes the dict without **.

knowledge_points.title: Unknown names become an error message
knowledge_points.practice: Predict call_tool results for known and unknown names; complete the guard line.

knowledge_points.title: Bad arguments: catch TypeError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results for missing, extra and misspelled arguments; write the except clause.

topics.title: Sending tool results back to the model
topics.summary: Append the assistant's tool-call message and one role 'tool' message per call (matched by tool_call_id, content as a string), ready for the next request.

knowledge_points.title: Keep the assistant's request in the history
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}]
message = tool_reply("get_weather", '{"city": "Paris"}')["choices"][0]["message"]
messages.append(message)
print(len(messages), messages[-1]["role"])  # 2 assistant
The model must see its own tool request in the history, unchanged, before the results. (tool_reply builds a canned response like the one in read_tool_calls.)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the roles in the list after appending; fix code that appends only the results.

knowledge_points.title: One tool message per call, matched by id
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messages.append(message)
for call in message["tool_calls"]:
    args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
    result = call_tool(call["function"]["name"], args)
    messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": result})
print(messages[-1])
# {'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'call_1', 'content': '18C in Paris'}
tool_call_id ties each result to its request; every call must get exactly one answer or the API rejects the next request.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the tool message for a given call and result; find the bug when a result is sent without its id.

knowledge_points.title: Content must be a string: json.dumps structured results
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which results need json.dumps; predict the content string for several results.

knowledge_points.title: Trace one full round
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# request 1: [user]                 -> reply: tool_calls get_weather(Paris)
# request 2: [user, assistant, tool] -> reply: "It is 18C in Paris."
messages = ["user", "assistant", "tool", "assistant"]
print(len(messages))  # 4
Tools are sent again with request 2; the model reads the tool result and answers in text.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill a trace table of the message list after each step of a two-tool round; order the steps of a round.

topics.title: The agent loop: ask, act, repeat until done
topics.summary: Write the loop at the heart of an AI agent: call the model, run any requested tools, append results, and stop on a text answer or a step limit; test it with a scripted fake model.

knowledge_points.title: A scripted fake model
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what successive calls return; write a script that makes two tool calls then answers.

knowledge_points.title: Stop when the reply has no tool calls
knowledge_points.practice: Predict one_step's result for canned replies; complete the stop condition.

knowledge_points.title: The full loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def run_agent(model_fn, messages, max_steps=20):
    for step in range(max_steps):
        message = model_fn(messages)["choices"][0]["message"]
        messages.append(message)
        calls = message.get("tool_calls") or []
        if not calls:
            return message["content"]
        for call in calls:
            args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
            result = call_tool(call["function"]["name"], args)
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": result})
    return "Stopped: too many steps"

script = [tool_reply("get_weather", '{"city": "Paris"}'), text_reply("It is 18C.")]
print(run_agent(scripted_model, [{"role": "user", "content": "Paris?"}]))  # It is 18C.
scripted_model is the fake from KP1. Each pass: ask, append the reply, run every tool call, append results; the history grows until the model answers.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the loop's lines (Parsons); trace the messages list through a two-step script.

knowledge_points.title: A step limit stops runaway agents
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the message count after n steps; fix a while True version that never stops.

topics.title: Safe file tools for a coding agent
topics.summary: Write the file tools of a coding agent so they can only touch a working directory, never crash, and return bounded text the model can read.

knowledge_points.title: Keep every path inside the working directory
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
def resolve(working_dir, rel_path):
    base = os.path.abspath(working_dir)
    target = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base, rel_path))
    if os.path.commonpath([base, target]) != base:
        return None
    return target

print(resolve("calculator", "pkg/big.txt") is None)  # False
print(resolve("calculator", "../secrets.txt"))      # None
abspath resolves '..'; commonpath shows whether the target is still under the base folder.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict resolve() for paths with '..', '.', and absolute paths; complete the guard line.

knowledge_points.title: Why startswith is not enough
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
base = "/proj/calc"
target = "/proj/calculator/notes.txt"
print(target.startswith(base))                    # True  (wrong!)
print(os.path.commonpath([base, target]) == base)  # False
A sibling folder whose name begins the same way passes a string check; compare whole path parts.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug in a startswith-based guard; give a path that slips past it.

knowledge_points.title: Return errors as text and cap the size
knowledge_points.worked_example:
MAX_CHARS = 10000

def get_file_content(working_dir, file_path):
    target = resolve(working_dir, file_path)
    if target is None or not os.path.isfile(target):
        return f'Error: cannot read "{file_path}"'
    with open(target) as f:
        content = f.read(MAX_CHARS + 1)
    if len(content) > MAX_CHARS:
        content = content[:MAX_CHARS] + "\n[...truncated]"
    return content

print(get_file_content("calculator", "../.env"))  # Error: cannot read "../.env"
print(len(get_file_content("calculator", "pkg/big.txt")))  # 10015
resolve() is the guard from KP1. A tool's output goes back into the context window, so huge files are cut; problems become messages, not crashes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results for missing, outside and oversized files; write write_file with the same guard.

knowledge_points.title: The program, not the model, picks the folder
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which parameters belong in the schema; fix a schema that lets the model set the directory.

topics.title: A tool that runs code: subprocess with limits
topics.summary: Write an agent tool that runs a Python file inside the working directory with a timeout and returns its stdout, stderr and exit code as one string.

knowledge_points.title: Only .py files inside the sandbox
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the check for several paths; add a check that the file exists.

knowledge_points.title: Run with a timeout and capture output
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import subprocess, sys

def text_to_textnodes(text):
    nodes = [TextNode(text, TextType.TEXT)]
    nodes = split_nodes_delimiter(nodes, "**", TextType.BOLD)
    nodes = split_nodes_delimiter(nodes, "_", TextType.ITALIC)
    nodes = split_nodes_delimiter(nodes, "`", TextType.CODE)
    nodes = split_nodes_image(nodes)
    nodes = split_nodes_link(nodes)
    return nodes

def props_to_html(self):     # inside class HTMLNode
        if self.props is None:
            return ""
        result = ""
        for key, value in self.props.items():
            result += f' {key}="{value}"'
        return result

A site published at user.github.io/repo/ needs basepath '/repo/'; locally it is '/'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict basepath for given command lines; fix an index that crashes with no arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Rewrite root links for the base path
knowledge_points.worked_example: html = 'Blog' basepath = "/repo/" html = html.replace('href="/', f'href="{basepath}').replace('src="/', f'src="{basepath}') print(html) # Blog Links that start at / would point outside the project's folder on the host; prefixing them fixes every page at once.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rewritten links; choose which links must not change (https://...).

knowledge_points.title: Preview locally, then publish
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 main.py
$ cd public && python3 -m http.server 8888
# open http://localhost:8888 in a browser
$ python3 main.py "/repo/"   # build for publishing (e.g. GitHub Pages from docs/)
http.server serves a folder as-is, exactly like a static host would.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the commands to build and preview; choose the URL to open.
